sentences.en: Today I went to the hospital to register, and the staff member asked me to leave a phone number.

t: to be used to; to be in the habit of
one (spoken form used in phone numbers)
sentences.en: When Chinese people say phone numbers, they're used to reading the digit 一 (yī) as 幺 (yāo), so that other people won't mishear it.

t: one (spoken form used in phone numbers)
sentences.en: So, when I say my number, I read every 'one' (一) in it as 'yāo' (幺).
The staff member listened and wrote at the same time, and quickly finished writing it down.
He read the number back once, and asked me if it was right.
I said: "Yes, that's exactly the number."
Later, he really did call me, asking me to go back to the hospital again next week.

vocab: one (spoken form used in phone numbers)

quiz.q: What did the staff member ask the narrator to leave?
How do Chinese speakers often read the digit '1' in a phone number?
What happened after the visit, according to the story?
a: He called and asked her to come back next week

grammar.e: For phone numbers, Chinese speakers often read the digit 一 (yī) as 幺 (yāo) instead, so it isn't confused with other numbers.
grammar.x: 习惯把数字一读成幺。— They're used to reading the digit one as yāo.

grammar.p: 把 + object + verb (the 把 construction)
grammar.e: 把 moves the object in front of the verb to show exactly what happens to it.
grammar.x: 他把号码读了一遍。— He read the number back once.

grammar.e: 才 here means 'only then' — used with 不会 to say doing something this way prevents a problem.
grammar.x: 这样别人才不会听错。— This way, other people won't mishear it.
